title: Scrape burnt pancakes off a griddle over the lip into its grease tray with a scraper
instruction: Scrape the griddle clean into the grease tray with the scraper.
context: Fast food cooks (O*NET 35-2011.00, about 670,000 US jobs, BLS) and restaurant cooks (35-2014.00, about 1.4 million) scrape the griddle between orders and at close. O*NET's tasks for fast food cooks include "Clean food preparation areas, cooking surfaces, and utensils" and "Operate large-volume cooking equipment, such as grills, deep-fat fryers, or griddles"; for restaurant cooks, "Inspect and clean food preparation areas, such as equipment, work surfaces, and serving areas". At breakfast, pancakes left on the heat while an order goes out burn onto the plate, and burnt food left there burns onto the next order. It is stuck to the steel, so the scraper's edge has to be held flat on the plate and driven into it to break it up; a lifted edge rides over it. What it pushes spills round the blade's ends, so strokes have to overlap, and the pile has to be pushed over the lip into the tray, not flicked off onto the line.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Griddle: an Assure Parts 177AOGT1227 range-top add-on griddle (27 x 12-1/4 in. overall; a 22-3/8 x 12-1/4 in. (56.8 x 31.1 cm) cooking surface of 7-gauge type 430 stainless; 1-1/2 in. (3.8 cm) splash guards on both sides and the far end; a 3 x 12-1/4 x 1-1/4 in. grease tray across the open near end), set on the bench on its frame with the plate's top 5.0 cm above the bench and clamped down (fixed), tray end toward the robot. The plate runs from x 15.0 (the lip over the tray) to 71.8 and from y -17.55 to 13.55. The tray runs from x 7.4 to 15.0, its floor 3.2 cm below the plate's top. In real trials the plate is bare type 430 stainless, unoiled and not seasoned (oil would weaken the wax's hold). The frame sits against two stop blocks on the bench (the plate's near right corner within 2 mm, the lip square within 0.5 degree, the plate's top 5.0 cm up within 2 mm and level). (2) Debris: four burnt silver-dollar pancakes stuck to the plate, 7.0 cm across and 5 mm thick, 55.5 g in all. In the simulator they are in four of the seven 2.75 in. (7 cm) cavities of a Norpro 957R silicone silver-dollar pancake mold (9.5 x 9 in.; cavities 8.0 cm apart, inferred from its size): two side by side, their near edges 1.0 cm from the lip (centers x 19.5, y -7.5 and 0.5), and two behind them, offset half a cavity (x 26.4, y -3.5 and 4.5). Each pancake is cracked into 22 fragments (about 1.2 cm across, 1 mm cracks), each bonded to the plate on its own and freed when pushed sideways harder than 12 N per m of its width across the stroke (0.11 to 0.21 N); once free it slides on the plate. The layout is the same every trial. Real trials use a fixed-recipe substitute made in about 15 minutes (README): black-dyed paraffin wax (Gulf Wax household paraffin, melt point about 54 to 58 degrees C; CandleScience black liquid dye), poured at 75 to 85 degrees C from a double boiler, 14.0 g (within 0.2 g, by weight on the balance) into each of the same four cavities with the mold set on the clean, unoiled plate at its marks (two near cavities' edges 1.0 cm from the lip, the right one's edge 6.55 cm from the right guard, within 2 mm), each cavity's spot first warmed to 40 to 45 degrees C with a Wagner HT1000 heat gun (infrared thermometer on a tape mark). The wax wets the steel and freezes onto it; the mold is lifted at 3 minutes and the discs cool 10 minutes, to 20 to 24 degrees C (room temperature). Each disc is used only when it has no lifted edge, its black area on the overhead photo is within 10% of its cavity's reference, and it holds a weighed 86 g proof load pulled across the plate for 10 s (the simulator's bond for one 7 cm row: 12 N/m x 0.07 m = 0.84 N). Simulator discs: 13.9 g each (0.9 g per cubic cm, wax), 5 mm thick at about 80% coverage; real discs 4.0 mm over the whole cavity (mass matched). (3) Scraper: a Dexter-Russell Basics P94850 4 in. griddle scraper: stiff stainless blade 10.2 cm wide (1.5 mm thick in the simulator), 21.6 cm overall, white polypropylene handle 11.4 cm long (3.0 x 2.4 cm in the simulator) in line with the blade, 136 g. It lies loose on the bench right of the griddle, edge toward the robot, resting on its edge and the handle's end, centered at x 25.0, y -25.5 (in real trials laid in an outline traced on the bench, within 5 mm and 3 degrees). Both arms start at their ready pose. The griddle is never heated on a burner (only the four pour spots are warmed, then cooled): the trial runs at room temperature, the same every trial (cooks scrape it warm).
scoring: Measured by mass, as shares of the debris (55.5 g in the simulator), from where each fragment ends up. In the tray means inside the tray's walls and below the plate's top. Off the griddle means outside its footprint (plate, tray and splash guards): on the bench, the floor, or carried off on the scraper. Everything else is left on the griddle. The trial scores 1.0 when at least 98% is in the tray and nothing is left on the griddle (every fragment off the plate; each is 0.8 to 1.7%), and the scraper has been set down on the bench off the griddle, released and still for 1 s. Set down: the point where its neck meets the handle less than 3 cm above the bench and outside the griddle's footprint; released: no gripper touching it; still: under 1 cm a second and 10 degrees a second. The job is not finished while the scraper is still in hand or lying on the griddle. It scores 0.75 when at least 90% is in the tray and at most 2% is left on the griddle (about one fragment: a single fragment left scores 0.75). It scores 0.5 when at least 60% is in the tray, and 0.25 when at least 25% is (about one pancake). Otherwise it scores 0. Doing nothing scores 0. Two caps apply to every score. More than 2% off the griddle (a fragment or two thrown onto the line) caps the score at 0.25. A gouge caps it at 0.5 for the rest of the trial: while the scraper is held and sliding with its edge on the plate (within 0.6 mm, about the simulator's resting gap; 1.0 mm once a stroke has begun), the blade over 70 degrees to the plate, or its edge tilted over 10 degrees so only one corner touches, for 1 cm or more of a stroke (a stand-in for chatter marks and scratches in the plate). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. In a real trial the same shares are weighed on a U.S. Solid USS-DBS66-20 balance (2,000 g by 0.01 g): the tray's gain (in the tray); every piece lifted off the plate, guards and blade with a razor scraper and brush (left on the griddle; a thin wax film is not a piece and is not counted); what is brushed off the catch sheets, bench, floor and scraper (off the griddle). Their sum is the total; a trial whose total is more than 5% off the four poured masses is repeated. The set-down is judged from the video. Top photos before and after, from a fixed overhead phone under a fixed raking light with a 1 cm grid, record what is left; a new scratch in the steel 1 cm or longer is the gouge. In a real trial, nothing left on the griddle means under 0.40 g left (less than the smallest simulated fragment, 0.42 g) and no piece 1 mm or larger on the plate, guards or blade (checked by eye under the raking light without wiping, against a steel rule and the 1 cm grid photo).
reset_notes: Weigh the tray's gain, empty and wipe it. Scrape the plate with the razor scraper, wipe the four disc spots with odorless mineral spirits, then dry, until the raking-light photo shows no particle 1 mm or larger and no wax film. With the wax kept melted all session, set the mold at its marks, warm each cavity's spot to 40 to 45 degrees C with the heat gun and pour 14.0 g of black wax at 75 to 85 degrees C into it, lift the mold at 3 minutes, let the discs cool 10 minutes to 20 to 24 degrees C, and check each disc (no lifted edge; black area within 10% of its reference; holds the 86 g proof load for 10 s). About 5 minutes for the reset and 15 for the debris. Clamp the griddle against its stops and lay the scraper in its outline. In simulation every trial starts with every fragment bonded in place and the tray empty.
fidelity: Real size and mass. Each pancake is 22 rigid fragments, each freed when the blade pushes past 12 N per m of its width (baked food soils on steel: 0.3 to 80 J/m2). Real trials: black paraffin discs poured on warmed steel (13.9 g sim, 14.0 g real; 5 mm sim vs 4.0 mm real), each holding an 86 g proof load (one 7 cm row of the sim bond). Friction: plate 0.15 to 0.2 (waxy film), pieces on steel 0.4 to 0.5. No heat. Rigid scraper. Gouge: a blade-angle rule.
